title: Microphase Partitioning and QoS Simulation for Mixed-Latency Workloads
creator: Asha Mehta
description: Investigate a microphase partitioning strategy and an offline QoS simulator to balance latency-sensitive small-chat requests with high-throughput long-generation requests. Produce a scheduler policy proposal and validate it with synthetic and logged workload replays.
background: We currently see tail latency spikes when mixed short and long sequences share serving pools. Existing phase-splitting approaches in other tickets improved fairness but either reduced throughput or required brittle heuristics. Kernel selection and attention-cost awareness are available hooks in the runtime but we lack a quantitative simulator to evaluate policies across realistic mixes and hardware kernels.
goals: Create a microphase partitioning model that subdivides prefill/decode into fine-grained subphases to reduce blocking of short queries
Build an offline QoS simulator that replays production traces with kernel-level cost models (attention cost, kv-cache hits, quantization impact)
Produce a candidate policy with concrete configuration knobs (min microphase share, hedging windows, opportunistic consolidation) and estimate cost/latency trade-offs
Ship a canary rollout plan for runtime-1.23 that validates production improvements on Dedicated pools
success_criteria: P50 for short-chat requests improves by >=20% in simulated mixed workloads
Aggregate token throughput decreases by no more than 5% for the evaluated mixes
No increase in error/retry rate in 72h canary runs
Clear operational indicators in Console: per-route tail latency down, per-token cost delta and autoscaler signals stable
proposed_design: Microphase partitioning: split prefill into microphases (~16-64 token windows) and interleave decode slots for short requests
QoS simulator: deterministic replay of trace segments with configurable kernel cost tables (attention matrix cost, KV cache hit/miss penalty, quantization multiplier)
Policy knobs: microphase_share (percentage of GPU time reserved for short-slot queues), hedged_prefill_deadline (ms), opportunistic_merge_threshold (tokens)
Routing integration: tie microphase admission to model variant cost profile so low-precision kernels can be opportunistically used for short queries
Fallback: if microphase backpressure > threshold, trigger canary fallbacks to prioritized kernel paths to preserve P99
experiments: Simulator build: implement kernel cost table derived from kernel-probe runs (see ENG-14207) and GPU profiler samples
Synthetic mixes: 90/10 short/long, 50/50, 10/90 with varying interarrival distributions and sequence length histograms
Trace replay: sample 48 hours of production traces from dedicated-pool-3 (anonymized) and validate simulator fidelity against wall-clock telemetry
A/B canary: deploy microphase policy to 5% of traffic on dedicated runtime with extra tracing and per-token attribution
measurements: Simulator metrics: predicted P50/P95/P99 per-route, predicted throughput (tokens/s), predicted GPU occupancy and kv-cache hit ratio
Validation metrics: observed vs predicted latency error < 10% for P50 and P95 on test slices
Canary metrics: enable Console dashboard showing split-by-model/per-route latency, cost-per-1e6-tokens, autoscaler scale events
Performance counters: kernel runtime distribution, attention matrix FLOPs per token, number of hedged replays
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (sim+bench): complete simulator and run synthetic mixes (target completion 2026-03-05)
Phase 1 (trace validation): run trace replays and refine kernel cost tables (2026-03-08 to 2026-03-12)
Phase 2 (internal canary): deploy to non-customer test clusters and run 24h soak (2026-03-16)
Phase 3 (customer canary): 5% traffic on dedicated pool, monitor 72h with rollback guardrails (2026-03-20)
Phase 4 (wider rollout): gradual increase to 50% after signatures from SRE and PM (target runtime-1.23 minor release)
Rollback criteria: P99 increase > 10% or production error rate uplift > 0.5% over baseline
open_questions: What microphase granularity minimizes context-switch overhead on our current kernel scheduler? (16 vs 32 vs 64 token windows)
Does opportunistic kernel switching cause excessive kv-cache eviction costs for long-running decodes?
How to encode per-model attention cost in the model catalog so the scheduler can make informed decisions at admission time?
Should hedged prefill be implemented at RPC layer or inside the runtime arbiter for tighter timing control?
blockers: Need updated kernel probe data from infra team (blocked on ENG-14207 follow-up),
Anonymized production trace access requires data-sanitization from Privacy team (ticket PM-4122)
risks: Over-partitioning microphases could increase kernel launch overhead and harm throughput
Policy complexity may make root-cause analysis harder for SRE during incidents
Kernel-level opportunistic switches might expose subtle quantization quality regressions for some customers
notes: Prefer building simulator as a separate Go tool with a JSON trace input so we can plug it into CI
Consider exporting simulator predictions to Console as a preflight feature for Dedicated customers
This work should inform Optimize recommendations: we can suggest microphase_share per-customer based on workload profile
